Chapter 6. The Practice of Tonglen—Breathing in Pain, Breathing Out Relief.
You know, there are times when the world just feels heavy. Maybe you’ve felt it too—like suffering is everywhere, and your first instinct is to close up, to protect yourself from all that pain. But what if there was a different way?
There’s an ancient practice that’s quietly revolutionary. Instead of shutting down, it asks you to open your heart. To breathe in the pain—yours and others’—and to breathe out relief and kindness. This is the heart of tonglen.
Picture this: someone sitting alone in the early morning, still feeling weighed down after a rough argument with someone they love. Their chest feels tight, and everything inside wants to push that pain away—to distract, to numb. But, instead, they try something new. With every in-breath, they imagine drawing in all that heaviness, every ache and bit of regret—not just their own, but also the pain of anyone who might be feeling the same. Then, with every out-breath, they gently send out a sense of comfort, a wish for healing, to themselves and to everyone who’s hurting.
At first, this might sound a little strange. Why would anyone want to breathe in pain? But as you settle into the rhythm of your breath, something begins to shift. The line between your pain and someone else’s starts to blur. What once felt so isolating suddenly feels more universal—like you’re part of something bigger. And just the simple act of sending out relief, even if it’s only in your imagination, brings a kind of warmth and a sense of agency.
There was a man, for example, who’d just lost his job. In the middle of a sleepless night, he tried tonglen. He pictured everyone who was anxious about their future, breathing in their fear, and breathing out hope. Did it solve all his worries? No. But it softened them. He felt less alone, and more connected to the world around him.
The thing is, tonglen isn’t about taking on more suffering than you can handle. It’s about recognizing that pain is something we all share—and realizing your heart is big enough to hold both suffering and compassion together. Most people don’t realize how powerful it is just to acknowledge pain, to meet it with kindness, and to wish real relief for everyone who’s struggling.
Over time, tonglen becomes a way of living with an open heart. It gently reminds you that even in your darkest moments, there’s always the possibility of connection—of giving and receiving compassion, one breath at a time.
